opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I hold these views with a lot of uncertainty, and I'm not a nanotechnology expert. But the basic reason is that once you have AI systems that can do research roughly as well as strong human scientists, the pace of progress stops being set by how many human researchers we have and how quickly they can think. You can run many copies, run them faster, and have them work in parallel on every piece of a problem at once.

Nanotechnology and uploading are areas where, at least in my view, the main bottleneck is intellectual. A huge design space, very hard modeling and simulation problems, many subtle experimental questions. Those are exactly the things that speed up dramatically if you have abundant cognitive labor. It's not like building a power plant, where much of the time is spent pouring concrete and getting permits.

There's also a feedback loop. Better AI gives you better tools for designing molecular machinery, simulating biology, and running automated experiments, and those tools in turn speed up the next round. Things that might look like a century of progress at the human rate could compress into a much shorter period.

The physical world does push back: experiments take time, fabrication takes time, and some things you just can't simulate your way past. So I don't think it's instantaneous. But I'd be surprised if the gap between "AI that's roughly at human research level" and "really transformative physical technologies" were as long as people often intuitively assume. And that's a big part of why I think the safety work needs to happen before we reach that point, not after.

r001.rationale: The response says progress could compress into a much shorter period, but does not argue that a two-decade transition would be rapid relative to humans’ ability to adapt.

r002.rationale: The response mentions simulation as a way to accelerate progress, but says experiments still take time and some things cannot be simulated away; it does not claim that much iteration could happen entirely in simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't expect them to happen fast in calendar time by default. What I expect is that once you have systems doing research at or above human level, running in parallel and much faster than us, the bottleneck shifts from "how many clever people are thinking about this" to "how quickly can you run experiments in the physical world." And the surprising thing to me is how little of nanotechnology or neuroscience is actually gated on physical experiments versus on understanding.

Take uploading. The hard part isn't scanning a brain. We can already slice and image tissue at synaptic resolution; it's slow and expensive, but it's engineering. The hard part is knowing what level of detail matters, what the right abstraction of a neuron is, how to go from a connectome plus some molecular annotations to a functioning simulation. Those are questions where a lot of the progress comes from thinking hard about existing data and designing much better, more targeted experiments. If you have a million extremely capable researchers who never sleep, they're going to compress decades of that into something much shorter, and then the experiments they do ask for will be far more informative per dollar.

Nanotechnology is similar. Molecular dynamics, protein design, understanding how to build structures atom by atom: these are heavily computational problems. The physical loop is "synthesize, measure, iterate," and the iteration cycle in chemistry is days, not years. So if you've got an AI system that gets the design right on the third try instead of the three hundredth, you've sped things up enormously without changing the physics.

So the picture isn't "these fields are easy." It's that both of them are mostly bottlenecked on intelligence and careful reasoning rather than on waiting for nature. And if you believe, as I do, that we're going to get very capable AI in the next decade or two, then the relevant question becomes what happens to fields that were gated on human cognition. I'd expect them to move at a pace that looks shocking from where we're standing now.

I'll add the caveat that I could be wrong about where the bottlenecks are. There might be some irreducibly slow physical steps, like growing enough biological samples or scaling up fabrication, that keep things at a human pace. But my default guess is that those are the exception, not the rule.

r001.rationale: The response says progress could look shocking and discusses AI arriving within a decade or two, but it does not compare a two-decade transition with humans’ ability to adapt to a changed world.

r002.rationale: The response describes computational work and simulations, but its iteration examples still involve physical experiments (“synthesize, measure, iterate”); it does not say that much experimental iteration could happen entirely in simulation.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate those two cases, because uploading could be substantially harder. But the basic reason to expect things to move quickly is that AI could accelerate the research process itself. You’re no longer relying only on a relatively small number of human scientists; you could have many systems working in parallel, proposing experiments, interpreting results, and designing better tools.

That doesn’t mean physical constraints disappear. You still have to build equipment and run experiments, and some experiments take a long time. So I’m less confident about a particular timeline than about the possibility of a large acceleration.

Uploading also requires understanding what details of the brain you need to preserve and finding a way to measure them. Those could be serious bottlenecks. My expectation is that, if we get AI that’s much better than us at scientific research, we shouldn’t assume these technologies will remain as far away as they look under today’s rate of progress.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible acceleration and uncertainty about timelines, but does not compare a two-decade transition with humans’ capacity to adapt.

r002.rationale: The response mentions experiments and physical constraints, but does not say that accurate physical simulations could allow much of the iteration to happen in simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that advances in AI could dramatically accelerate the research needed to get there. Nanotechnology and uploading are hard problems, but a lot of that difficulty is in figuring out how to do them. If you have systems that can do that intellectual work much faster than humans, the timeline could shrink substantially.

That doesn’t mean everything becomes instantaneous. You still need experiments, equipment, and manufacturing, and those have physical constraints. But I wouldn’t assume those constraints preserve the decades-long timelines we might expect from human researchers. The claim is more that once AI can substantially automate science and engineering, our usual intuitions about how long these developments take become much less reliable.

r001.rationale: It says AI could shrink timelines and make usual intuitions about decades-long timelines unreliable, but does not argue that a two-decade transition would be rapid relative to humans’ capacity to adapt to a changed world.

r002.rationale: It mentions experiments and physical constraints but does not explain that sufficiently accurate physical simulations could allow much experimental iteration to happen entirely in simulation.
